identity.title: Pain out of proportion to examination findings

technique.how: Ask the patient to rate pain severity and observe distress, analgesic requirement and inability to lie still, then compare with the examined area: abdomen soft with little tenderness (mesenteric ischemia) or skin with pain extending beyond visible erythema and exquisite tenderness disproportionate to a modest cellulitis (necrotizing infection).
technique.prerequisites: Examine before heavy opioid dosing if possible; document extent of erythema with a marker and time.

interpretation.positive_finding: Severe pain with a benign abdomen in a patient with atrial fibrillation, vascular disease or low-flow state should be treated as mesenteric ischemia until CT angiography excludes it; in skin infection it raises the odds of necrotizing fasciitis about 4.5-fold versus cellulitis.
interpretation.negative_finding: Pain proportional to findings does not exclude either diagnosis; no single feature has adequate sensitivity to rule out necrotizing fasciitis, and mesenteric ischemia often presents with vague signs.
interpretation.pitfalls: Elderly, diabetic and obtunded patients underreport pain; late ischemia with peritonitis makes the exam 'proportionate' again. In necrotizing infection, anesthesia of the skin can replace pain late in the course.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: CT angiography for suspected mesenteric ischemia, or urgent surgical exploration/consult for suspected necrotizing infection; do not wait for labs.

estimates.population: necrotizing fasciitis cases admitted to a tertiary hospital 2004-2013, each matched to two cellulitis controls (retrospective case-control)
estimates.reference_standard: surgical/histological diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis versus clinically diagnosed cellulitis
estimates.quote: The clinical features that most significantly increased the odds of NF were recent surgery (LR+ 7.0) pain-out-of-proportion (LR+ 4.5)

sources.citation: Alayed KA, Tan C, Daneman N. Red Flags for Necrotizing Fasciitis: A Case Control Study. Int J Infect Dis. 2016.
Cudnik MT, Darbha S, Jones J, Macedo J, Stockton SW, Hiestand BC. The diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2014.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a 'proportionate' exam to defer imaging in an elderly patient with atrial fibrillation, recent MI, heart failure or dialysis who has acute severe abdominal pain.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Suspected necrotizing fasciitis or mesenteric ischemia is a surgical emergency; mesenteric ischemia carries pooled operative mortality of 47%.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: 'Out of proportion' is a subjective judgment with no published reliability data found; Alayed's feature was abstracted retrospectively from charts.

extraction_notes: Necrotizing fasciitis: Alayed 2016 is a retrospective matched case-control, so only LR+ (4.5) is entered; no CI or sensitivity given per feature in the abstract, and the abstract states 'no individual findings with sufficient sensitivity to rule out NF (sensitivity <= 85% and LR- >= 0.5 for all findings)' (Abstract). Prevalence not entered (case-control). Mesenteric ischemia: Cudnik 2014 meta-analysis pooled only lactate, D-dimer and CT; the abstract concludes 'Signs, symptoms, and laboratory testing are insufficiently diagnostic for the condition' and provides no pooled estimate for pain out of proportion, so no mesenteric-ischemia estimate is entered. Mortality figure in escalation_warning: 'pooled operative mortality rate for mesenteric ischemia was 47% (95% CI = 40% to 54%)' (Cudnik, Abstract).
